description: We are a passionate team of 6 aspiring engineers participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are interested in AI/ML, software development, space technology, healthcare innovation and problem-solving. Our goal is to build ASTRA-VITAL, an innovative astronaut health monitoring solution, and compete for global judging. We welcome enthusiastic teammates skilled in Python, React, AI/ML, UI/UX, data science, research and presentation.
summary:
**AEGIS-V — Astronaut Health & Life-Support Intelligence System**, developed by Team VITRAXIS, is a prototype designed to support astronaut health and safety during space missions. It brings together 18 health and environmental indicators, including heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, radiation exposure, cabin CO₂, sleep, fatigue, hydration, and nutrition, in one integrated platform.

AEGIS-V goes beyond displaying readings. It uses deterministic rule-based alerts to highlight potential concerns, while AI-assisted explanations help astronauts understand reported changes and possible next steps. It also provides structured emergency medical guidance, incident documentation, life-safety monitoring, and selected offline mission-continuity workflows.

The project addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health in environments where medical assistance and communication with Earth may be limited. By making health information easier to interpret and supporting organised responses to potential emergencies, AEGIS-V aims to help crews make more informed decisions and maintain mission readiness.

**AEGIS-V is a research prototype, not a clinically validated or flight-certified medical system.**
details:
What AEGIS-V Does

AEGIS-V is an astronaut health and mission-safety support platform developed by Team VITRAXIS. It brings 18 health and environmental indicators into one interface, covering vital signs, cabin conditions, sleep, fatigue, vision-related indicators, nutrition, and hydration.

The system follows a structured workflow: Monitor → Validate → Analyze → Explain → Respond → Follow Up. Deterministic rule-based logic identifies potential concerns and generates alerts. Gemini-powered AI features assist with explaining health information, answering user questions, and supporting voice transcription. The platform also includes emergency-response guidance, incident documentation, a Life-Safety Sentinel, medical-kit information, and selected local workflows designed to remain useful during simulated communication interruptions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronauts operate in an environment where distance, communication delays, isolation, and limited medical resources can make health decisions difficult. AEGIS-V aims to make important health information easier to understand, help crews recognise potential concerns, and support more organised responses when immediate assistance from Earth is unavailable.

Its intended impact is to strengthen crew awareness, support timely decision-making, improve emergency preparedness, and contribute to safer, more resilient human space missions.

Technology Used

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite
  • Backend: Node.js, Express, TypeScript
  • Authentication and cloud storage: Firebase Authentication and Cloud Firestore
  • Local persistence: IndexedDB for selected records and offline action queues
  • AI: Google Gemini API for assistant responses, triage explanations, and voice transcription
  • Application logic: Deterministic rule-based alerting and health-data workflows

The prototype uses simulated demonstration telemetry and a synthetic 14-day baseline. It does not claim live NASA telemetry, integrated spacecraft sensors, or clinically validated medical thresholds.

Creativity and Design Considerations

AEGIS-V is designed to go beyond a conventional vital-sign dashboard. Its distinctive approach combines health monitoring, explainable AI assistance, structured emergency workflows, and selected mission-continuity features in one astronaut-focused interface.

Our team considered the constraints of space missions: limited access to medical support, communication interruptions, crew workload, clarity under stress, data reliability, privacy, and the need to distinguish measured or entered information from simulated data. We prioritised understandable alerts and actionable guidance over simply displaying more readings.

AEGIS-V is a research prototype intended to demonstrate this approach. It is not a medical diagnosis system, a flight-certified product, or a replacement for professional medical protocols.
